```{r knitr-setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    comment = "#",
    prompt = FALSE,
    tidy = FALSE,
    cache = FALSE,
    collapse = TRUE
)

old <- options(width = 100L)
```

```{r library}
library(pubflow)
library(ggplot2)
```

[Get started](v01-get-started.html) built a table, a figure and a text in three
steps of a pipeline. This vignette looks at these outputs in turn: what they are,
how you set them up and how the pieces of a document refer to each other. The
steps that return them are ordinary pipeflow steps (see pipeflow's
[Get started](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v01-get-started.html));
the vignette on documents and layout steps shows how to arrange the
outputs into a document.

An output is a plain R object with *metadata*: a table is a huxtable, a figure a
ggplot or a recorded plot, a text a character string. Functions that read the
object, e.g. `print()` or `summary()`, work as on the object without the metadata.

The examples show outputs one at a time, each as a small document rendered to
HTML. They use this helper:

```{r show-doc, eval = FALSE}
show_doc <- function(...) pub_html(pub_doc(...))
```

```{r show-doc-framed, echo = FALSE}
# The same as show_doc() above, but framed to set the outputs apart from the
# vignette's own text, and with their headings left out of the table of contents
# of the pkgdown site
show_doc <- function(...) {
    html <- pub_html(pub_doc(...))
    htmltools::div(
        style = "border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 0 1em;",
        htmltools::attachDependencies(
            htmltools::HTML(gsub("<h([1-6])", "<h\\1 data-toc-skip", html)),
            htmltools::htmlDependencies(html)
        )
    )
}
```

## Tables

`pub_table()` builds a table from a data.frame. We summarise the ozone
concentration of New York in `airquality` by month:

```{r monthly}
monthly <- aggregate(Ozone ~ Month, data = airquality, FUN = function(x) {
    c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
}) |>
    do.call(what = data.frame)
names(monthly) <- c("month", "n", "mean", "sd")
monthly$n <- as.integer(monthly$n)
monthly$month <- month.name[monthly$month]
monthly
```

A table gets a caption, readable column labels and the number of decimal places
of the numeric columns:

```{r table}
tab <- pub_table(
    monthly,
    caption = "Ozone concentration by month",
    labels = c(month = "Month", n = "N", mean = "Mean (ppb)", sd = "SD (ppb)"),
    digits = c(mean = 1L, sd = 1L)
)
show_doc(tab)
```

Columns without `digits` get the number format of the table theme (four decimal
places by default), and whole numbers like `n` get none.

The result is a [huxtable](https://hughjonesd.github.io/huxtable/) and can be
used as such. `pub_table()` only sets it up: a header and body, a theme and the
number formats. The cells keep the values and are formatted when the table is
rendered, by the same code for every format (HTML, Word, PDF), so that a table shows the
same text everywhere. `pub_cell_text()` returns this text:

```{r cell-text}
pub_cell_text(tab)
```

### Headers, footnotes and merged cells

More arguments structure the table: `header` puts a spanner above columns with
equal labels, `footnotes` adds numbered footnotes below the table, `merge` joins
consecutive equal cells of a column and `na` is the text for missing values. Here
the data are the coefficients of a linear model of the ozone concentration, one
fit per month:

```{r structure}
fits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(airquality, airquality$Month), function(d) {
    fit <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = d)
    ci <- confint(fit)
    data.frame(
        month = month.name[d$Month[1L]],
        term = c("Intercept", "Temp"),
        estimate = coef(fit),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
}))
fits <- fits[fits$month %in% c("May", "June"), ]

pub_table(
    fits,
    caption = "Linear model of ozone by temperature",
    labels = c(
        month = "Month",
        term = "Term",
        estimate = "Estimate",
        lower = "Lower",
        upper = "Upper"
    ),
    digits = c(estimate = 2L, lower = 2L, upper = 2L),
    header = c(lower = "95% CI", upper = "95% CI"),
    footnotes = c(estimate = "Least squares fit, one per month."),
    merge = "month"
) |>
    show_doc()
```

`?pub_table` lists the other arguments: alignment, column widths, font size and
the table `theme`. A theme sets font size, borders (style, colour, width) and the
default number format for all tables, and can carry a `style` function for a
house look that depends on the role of a row, e.g. a coloured header. Use
`options(pubflow.table_theme = pub_table_theme(...))` to change it for the whole
session.

### Style cells with huxtable

pubflow has no functions of its own to style cells, use
[huxtable's](https://hughjonesd.github.io/huxtable/reference/index.html), e.g.
`set_bold()`, `set_text_color()` or the mapping functions like `map_text_color()`.
Two things to keep in mind:

* The rows of huxtable's functions include the header rows. `pub_table_rows()`
  gives the table rows of the header, body and footnotes, so the body row `i` is
  the table row `pub_table_rows(tab)$body[i]`.
* Give rows as integer indices (or names), not as a logical vector:
  huxtable recycles a short logical vector, also into the footnote rows.

Here the months with a mean above 40 ppb are set in bold red:

```{r style}
high <- pub_table_rows(tab)$body[monthly$mean > 40]

tab |>
    huxtable::set_bold(high, huxtable::everywhere) |>
    huxtable::set_text_color(high, huxtable::everywhere, "darkred") |>
    show_doc()
```

Call huxtable's functions with the `huxtable::` prefix, as other packages
(flextable) mask some of their names.

### Struck-through cells

`pub_strikeout()` strikes cells through, e.g. for excluded measurements. It shows
the text of the cells as they are formatted, so strike through *last*, after all
number formats are set:

```{r strikeout}
runs <- data.frame(
    sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
    result = c(0.8, 12.25, 0.95),
    excluded = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
tabRuns <- pub_table(
    runs[, c("sample", "result")],
    caption = "Assay results",
    digits = c(result = 2L)
)
rows <- pub_table_rows(tabRuns)$body[runs$excluded]
tabRuns |>
    huxtable::set_text_color(rows, huxtable::everywhere, "grey50") |>
    pub_strikeout(rows) |>
    show_doc()
```

Word, PDF and HTML all show the cells struck through. There is no underline.

### Combining tables

Combine the *data* and build the table once, rather than gluing finished tables
together: bind the data of several batches with `rbind()` and give
`pub_table(merge = "batch")`, or subset the data to get one table per batch.

If you do combine finished tables with huxtable's `rbind()`, `cbind()` or `[`,
the cell styles are kept, but the pieces are bound by position, each keeps its
own borders and the metadata of the table (see below) get lost, except for
`rbind()`, which keeps those of the first table. Finish the result with
`pub_table()` again and set the footnotes, widths and metadata on the final table.

## Rounding

Numbers in tables are rounded *half away from zero* on their decimal text, as in
the USP General Notices (7.20) and SAS's `ROUND()`: if the first dropped digit is
5 or more, the last digit goes up. R's `round()`, `sprintf()` and `formatC()`
round the binary value instead and send exact ties to the even digit:

```{r round}
x <- c(0.125, 2.675, -2.675, 9.995)
round(x, 2)
pub_round(x, 2)
```

Use the same rules wherever a number appears outside a table. `pub_round()`
returns the rounded numbers, e.g. to compare a result with a limit that is
specified with a number of decimal places. `pub_format_num()` returns the text that
a table cell would show, so you can quote a number in a text and it matches the
table:

```{r format-num}
pub_format_num(x, 2)
pub_format_num(mean(c(98.25, 99.1)), "Mean assay: %.2f %%")
```

A format is a number of decimal places or a `sprintf()` format with exactly one
`%.nf`, `%.ne` or `%.ng` conversion (`?pub_round`). The `number_format` of a
table theme accepts the same; `digits` of `pub_table()` takes decimal places
only.

## Figures

A plot is a figure without further ado: a ggplot or a recorded base plot
(`grDevices::recordPlot()`) in a document is shown as a figure. `pub_figure()`
adds a caption, a size or other metadata. Image files need it, as otherwise their
paths would be taken as text:

```{r figure}
trend_plot <- function(data) {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(.data$Temp, .data$Ozone)) +
        geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE)
    pub_figure(
        p,
        caption = "Ozone concentration by temperature",
        width = 6,
        height = 3.5
    )
}
fig <- trend_plot(airquality)
show_doc(fig)
```

The size is in inches (default 8 x 6) and sets the proportions of the plot in the
document; `out_width = "60%"` shrinks the figure relative to the text width.

As in Get started, the function that makes the plot is defined outside the
pipeline: a ggplot keeps the environment it was made in, so a plot made by code
inside a pipeline's constructor would hold the whole pipeline in every copy.

Image files, e.g. made by another program, are figures too. Give one file, or
several files of the same plot, e.g. a png and a pdf. Each output format takes
the file that suits it: HTML and Word show the png (or jpg), a PDF made with LaTeX
can use the vector file (see `?pub_figure`).

```{r figure-file, eval = FALSE}
pub_figure(c("trend.png", "trend.pdf"), caption = "Trend")
```

### Figures rendered in the step

Usually a plot is drawn when the document is rendered. With `render = TRUE`,
`pub_figure()` draws it right away, at its size and 200 dpi, and returns the png
image with the metadata:

```{r figure-render}
png <- pub_figure(fig, render = TRUE)
png
pub_type(png)
```

Use it in steps that run in other R processes (workers) and for pipelines that
are saved with `saveRDS()`. A ggplot holds environments, so a copy of it is no
longer identical to the original, and the document draws it again although nothing
changed. The image survives copying unchanged, so the document uses it as it is:

```{r figure-copy}
identical(fig, unserialize(serialize(fig, NULL)))
identical(png, unserialize(serialize(png, NULL)))
```

Recorded base plots need it too, as they can't be replayed in another R session.
The price: the image can't be changed by later steps, so the step that renders
it should be the last that touches the figure, and its size is fixed (use
`out_width` to scale it in the document). A report with vector figures
(`figure = list(device = "pdf")`) still shows the png. Caption, `id` and other
metadata can be set as for any figure:

```{r figure-render-show}
show_doc(pub_figure(png, caption = "Ozone concentration by temperature (rendered)"))
```

## Texts

A text is a character vector in Markdown. `pub_text()` joins the lines and
checks the Markdown:

```{r text}
txt <- pub_text(
    c(
        "The model explains **49%** of the variance ($R^2 = 0.49$).",
        "",
        "- the data are from May to September 1973",
        "- missing ozone values are left out",
        "",
        "Complete the discussion: [<insert text>]{.placeholder}"
    ),
    title = "Summary"
)
show_doc(txt)
```

The supported Markdown is the same in all formats: paragraphs, emphasis, code,
links, bullet and numbered lists, line breaks, inline and display math and code
blocks. A *placeholder* (`[<insert text>]{.placeholder}`) marks a gap that someone
fills in by hand, e.g. in the Word report. It is highlighted in every format. A
heading is an error, as the structure of a document comes from its sections
(see the vignette on documents and layout steps):

```{r text-heading, error = TRUE}
pub_text(c("# Results", "Some text"))
```

Format numbers in a text with `pub_format_num()` (see above), so that they agree
with the tables. A step can also return a plain character vector, which is
checked in the same way when it is put into a document.

## Metadata

Each output carries metadata, a named list in the attribute `pubflow`.
`pub_table()`, `pub_figure()` and `pub_text()` set it for you, and
`pub_meta()` reads it:

```{r meta}
pub_type(fig)
pub_meta(fig)
pub_meta(tab, "caption")
```

`pub_type()` tells what a document makes of an object: a table, figure, text or
a few other types. `pub_set_meta()` sets or removes single entries, e.g. a `title`
that is shown above the item, `landscape = TRUE` to place it on landscape pages
(Word and PDF) or `locked = TRUE` to lock it in Word against accidental edits.
Keys that pubflow doesn't know are kept, so you can add your own.

```{r set-meta}
tab <- pub_set_meta(tab, title = "Monthly summary", id = "monthly")
pub_meta(tab)
```

The metadata of a huxtable are kept by `rbind()`, but not by `[` and `cbind()`,
see [Combining tables](#combining-tables). `?pub_meta` lists the keys.

## Cross-references

A text can refer to a table or figure: `@tab:<id>` and `@fig:<id>` stand for
"Table 1" or "Figure 2" and link to the item with that `id` in its metadata. The
item needs a caption, as only captions are numbered, and its `id` must be unique in
the document. The ids start with a letter, end with a letter or digit and
contain only letters, digits, `_` and `-`:

```{r crossref}
fig <- pub_set_meta(fig, id = "trend")

txt <- pub_text(c(
    "@tab:monthly lists the ozone concentration by month, @fig:trend shows",
    "how it depends on the temperature."
))
show_doc(txt, tab, fig)
```

In a Word report these are cross-reference fields, in LaTeX and Typst
references, in HTML links, and the numbering is the engine's own. So the numbers
stay right when someone moves a figure in Word and updates the fields. The word
before the number ("Table", "Figure") comes from the `labels` of the report
spec (see `?pub_report_spec`). Only texts contain references; captions, titles
and table cells show `@fig:x` as it is. Text in code, math, placeholders and links
is left alone, as are `\@fig:x` and `a@fig:x`.

A reference that can't be resolved (unknown id, missing caption, a duplicate id)
is an error when you write a report with `pub_render()`, listing all problems, so
that a broken reference never goes unnoticed. `pub_html()` and the viewer only warn
and show the reference as marked text, so that a draft still displays:

```{r crossref-broken}
broken <- pub_text("See @fig:missing.")
html <- pub_html(pub_doc(broken))
```
